claims.claim: The hydrator's commit server is the single push path for every hydrated branch (RFC-002 delegates the actual push operation to it), and the signing proposal makes that component fail at startup when `commitserver.sign.hydrated.commits` is on and the mounted GPG key is missing or invalid, with no silent fallback. A rotated or mis-mounted key therefore stops hydration for every Application at once, and the only detection signal is a commit-server crashloop in the Argo CD namespace: downstream Applications stay `Synced` against their last hydrated commit, so no app-level health or sync alert fires while the fleet quietly goes stale.

RFC-002's push-to-stage mode names an unspecified 'external system to move changes to the deployment branch' as the integration point, and the platform sync notes identify what that system actually is here: the stage-branch promoter, still a shell script that nobody owns. The design's promotion step has no on-call owner, so a promoter failure at night has no named responder and no runbook.

The failure signal of that unowned promoter is a successful-looking deploy, not an error. T-26443 reports that in push-to-stage mode an auto-sync Application immediately syncs whatever the stage branch last held because the external promoter has not yet moved the fresh manifests; combined with the promoter being an unowned shell script, a promoter outage silently deploys old manifests while the Application reports `Synced`. There is no alert on this path; detection is a human noticing the wrong version in the cluster.

The progressive-sync false-complete failure has no detection path at all. T-27949 shows the ApplicationSet reporting `status.applicationStatus` `Healthy` and the rollout complete while child Applications are `OutOfSync` with no sync operation created, and notes that ApplicationSet controller logs were at warn level so no progressive-sync transition logs were emitted. T-27846 confirms the missing instrumentation: the metrics that would answer 'my sync is not starting, why / which Applications is it waiting for?' are still only a proposal. So neither the status field, nor logs, nor metrics surface the condition — it is found by a person opening the child Application.

The interim restriction from the incident review — hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until there is a debounce, because each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave — exists only as a line in raw review notes. The pilot ticket T-27949 still records source-hydrator piloting on a RollingSync ApplicationSet without carrying the restriction, and there is no controller-level check to enforce it. The next team that enables both hits the wave-restart loop with nothing in the ticket or the product to stop them.

The standing incident mitigation is unreachable through any supported operator surface. The runbook rule is to switch the ApplicationSet to `AllAtOnce` deletion before deleting any child app by hand, but the roadmap states that first-class UI/CLI/API support for ApplicationSet resources does not include managing deletion order of child applications, leaving teardown a manual operator action. The night-shift responder must hand-edit `strategy.deletionOrder` in the ApplicationSet CR with kubectl; the mitigation depends on a control the roadmap says will not be built.

Ordered deletion is shipping without a recovery path for its own mid-way failure. The PRD's `Reverse` deletionOrder waits for one application to be fully deleted before moving to the next, and T-28511 shows exactly that wait failing to complete when a child is stuck `Progressing`, leaving the wave restarting from the top. The dedicated rollback work for hydrated sources (T-27327, which would render the History & Rollback tab's rollback directly to the sync branch) has been deprioritized to next quarter, so an operator interrupted mid-teardown has no product-level revert — only manual git surgery on the sync branch.

The agreed rollout control and the feature's actual kill switch do not match. RFC-001 states as a goal that impersonation can be enabled or disabled only at the system level, applicable to all Argo CD Applications once flipped, while the platform sync call decided impersonation goes behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide. Operationally this means the documented rollback for an impersonation regression is a fleet-wide disable of `application.sync.impersonation.enabled`, affecting every tenant, not the per-project backout the rollout plan assumes exists.

Server-Side Diff on external clusters creates an open-ended recurring support task, not a one-time grant. T-28695 records five rounds of adding `patch` rules to a least-privilege cluster role, each triggered by a new chart introducing a resource kind that produces a `ComparisonError`, with no end state — every new chart is a new ticket. The same error string arrives from a second component in T-26271, where the failure is the CLI diff path through `argocd-server` in-cluster; identical symptoms from two different code paths mean each incoming report costs a triage step to decide which one it is before any fix applies.

T-26271's root cause was established on the platform sync call — with impersonation enabled the diff runs as the destination service account, which does not hold `patch` on cluster-scoped resources — but the notes record that someone still needs to write it on the ticket, and the ticket itself still reasons from the broad cluster Secret credential and asks why the diff suddenly runs with a narrower identity. The diagnosis exists and the ticket does not carry it, so the reporter keeps chasing the cluster Secret and every future responder re-derives the same answer.

A single broken diff becomes uncontainable load on the weakest cluster. T-28695 describes the Application rotating `Synced` ↔ `Unknown` on every reconcile, meaning the application controller re-issues server-side apply dry-runs against the external cluster continuously rather than once. T-29001 establishes that the only rate-limiting knobs are the global `controller.k8s.client.qps` and `controller.k8s.client.burst`, which apply to all managed destination clusters, and that edge clusters can be overwhelmed by the defaults during intense discovery. The operator's only lever to protect a fragile cluster from one app's diff churn is to slow reconciliation for every cluster.
